title: Williams to stage London display for 50th anniversary celebrations
author: The Race Team
text:
The Williams Formula 1 team will mark its 50th anniversary with what it calls "year-long celebrations" of its heritage, headlined by a commemorative display in London.

Six cars that represent significant moments in both Williams and F1 history will be part of the team's 'W50 Live' display at 26 Leake Street in central London, off Waterloo's iconic under-station graffiti tunnel, alongside an F1 showcar complete with the team's 2027 livery.

The car that uses that livery in competition will be known as the FW50 , Williams has officially announced.

That is in keeping with its famous FW chassis moniker, in honour of founder Frank Williams, as the team 'skips' the FW49 name to mark the 50th anniversary of the F1 team's first race in 1977, when it ran as Williams Grand Prix Engineering.

The Leake Street display - which runs from February 11-28 and will be open to the public as a ticketed event - will include the first F1 car produced by Williams Grand Prix Engineering, the FW06, as well as the FW11B, FW14B, and FW19 cars driven to world championship success by Nelson Piquet in 1987, Nigel Mansell in 1992, and Jacques Villeneuve in 1997 respectively.

Williams has chosen to also note two F1 milestones with its other two car choices: the 2003 FW25 set the record for the fastest average speed in F1 history through Juan Pablo Montoya, which stood for 17 years, while 2016's FW38 still has the record for the highest speed ever reached by an F1 car, when Valtteri Bottas hit 378km/h (234.9mph) during that year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend.

It will also give fans the chance to choose the livery for its home race, the British GP at Silverstone. This is believed to be a full branding takeover including Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz's racesuits, team kit and garage as well as the car.

Limited-edition merchandise to honour "some of the standout moments, personalities and car designs that have made Williams what it is today" will be produced, including a W50 Monopoly set that is due to go on sale before Christmas.

Williams has promised there are "many more 50th anniversary moments to be revealed over the coming months".

Tickets for the 'W50 Live' event will go on pre-sale later this month. Members of Williams's W Club will have access to this on October 26, before a general sale follows on October 29. More information can be found at williamsf1.com/w50live

title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt
author: Kalyeena Makortoff
text:
Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as global investors fret over potential interest rate hikes

Larry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is coming

An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.

Some of those semiconductor stocks, such as SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, plunged nearly 11% and 9.5%, respectively. The index closed at a six-month low, down 8.1%.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by 4.9% on Thursday, after an 11% slump in memory chip maker Kioxia and a 10% drop in SoftBank, a big investor in ChatGPT owner OpenAI.

The falls followed a slide on Wall Street during the previous day’s session, where the Nasdaq Composite fell by 1.9% and the S&P 500 dropped 1.1%, logging its worst performance since July.

The sell-off comes after US data showed stateside inflation jumped to a higher than expected 3.7% in September , marking the fastest increase in prices since the consumer price index (CPI) rate hit a three-year peak of 4.2% in May.

The figure has rattled investors who are now expecting fresh interest rate increases by the US Federal Reserve, with some punters pricing in another increase as soon as the end of the month.

“Markets have just had an incredibly tumultuous 24 hours, as a strong US CPI print was then followed up with mounting fears around the AI trade,” Deutsche Bank analysts led by Jim Reid, said.

Worryingly, the figures showed this was not about fuel costs, which have been pushed up by geopolitical tensions including the ripple effects from the US war on Iran. Reid said: “This wasn’t just an energy surge driving prices higher, as there were broad-based moves across the consumer basket.”

The sell-off follows warnings from the International Monetary Fund, which said earlier this week that the threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk.

“The consequences of an AI correction could be global,” it warned. Aside from the US, Asian markets would be most exposed, with the UK and eurozone potentially more insulated – although investors with US holdings would be hit.

The latest jitters hit China, where Shanghai’s CSI 300 slipped as much as 2.4%, marking the lowest level since August 2025. In Taiwan, one of the world’s leading chip makers and Asia’s most valuable company, TSMC, fell 2% despite reporting its sixth straight quarter of profits.

European stocks were skewing lower at the start of trading, with the Europe Stoxx 600 down by 0.4%, the UK’s FTSE 100 down 0.06%, France’s CAC 40 down 0.19%, and Spain’s Ibex falling 0.17%. Germany’s DAX fell by 0.53%.

In the US, stock futures pointed to losses for tech stocks, with the Nasdaq 100 futures dropping 1%.

title: Our verdict on Haas signing Camara for F1 2027
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Is that a good move? What can we expect from Camara, and what does it mean for his 2027 team-mate Ollie Bearman?

Here's what our team thinks:

A fantastic wildcard addition to F1's 2027 grid

If Rafael Camara is as exciting as I've been told he looked in his Haas F1 test debut, then he is a fantastic wildcard addition to the F1 grid.

His credentials from his junior career make him a worthy graduate anyway. This is a driver who was among the best in karting, and has now pieced together a rare run of consecutive titles higher and higher up the single-seater ladder.

Winning championships is never easy but that alone isn't a guarantee of the kind of ability or traits that will then thrive in F1. The work done in F1 machinery, even in brief opportunities, often counts for far more.

Haas was obviously aware Camara was a promising prospect from his feeder series CV. But, I'm told, it was won over comprehensively when Camara drove its car at Portimao. He was so fast that some in Haas believe that Ollie Bearman - who drove briefly on the day to establish a reference - wouldn't have been as quick even with a proper runplan.

That's not to say Camara is faster or a better prospect than Bearman. But he's that level: rapid, and with an instantly good impression. So it will be fascinating to see if this translates.

Where he's a gamble most is his racecraft and decision-making, which is unpolished based on his Formula 2 error rate - although, ironically, that's something that went for Bearman in his rookie season last year too...

This is the next proper test of Bearman's credentials as a potential future Ferrari F1 driver.

It's almost seemed pre-ordained since he burst onto the scene in Saudi Arabia as the stand-in for Carlos Sainz while Sainz had his appendix removed.

The performances Bearman put up against Nico Hulkenberg, while Kevin Magnussen was suspended and then unwell, only strengthened the feeling Bearman is something special and would eventually replace Lewis Hamilton at the Scuderia.

Bearman has seen off Esteban Ocon fairly comfortably, in terms of raw speed at least. I do think Ocon's greater experience has helped the team, but Ocon isn't overall fast enough, consistently enough, versus Bearman to justify what Haas was paying him, as well as the spiky attitude Ocon apparently had behind the scenes within that team.

Camara brings a new dimension - another highly-rated F2 graduate, with similar Ferrari Academy support that propelled Bearman to F1, and there's the added dynamic of Camara's impressive Testing of Previous Cars performance at Portimao.

Camara hasn't gone properly head-to-head with Bearman yet, but there's no doubt in my mind that (commercial considerations aside) Haas feels it now has a driver on its books that it expects to give Bearman a properly hard time.

If the hype isn't real, then Bearman has nothing to fear, but if Camara is as good as he appears to be from what we've heard so far then Bearman is going to need to find another gear in 2027.

His mission is to stop Camara from becoming the new flavour of the month, ultimately trying to make sure the next new kid on the block doesn't reach Ferrari before he does.

The ideal driver line-up for Haas

This feels like the ideal driver line-up vibe for a team in Haas's position - a well-established underdog that can score semi-regularly if its drivers maximise their chances and fortune falls its way.

Two drivers trying to climb over each other to prove themselves to F1's most legendary team, which also happens to be the top squad most likely to have a vacancy in the medium-term future given Hamilton's career position. There's everything to fight for and zero risk of complacency.

Plus, Bearman is now relatively experienced enough to lean on as a quasi-leader/benchmark.

Last time Haas went all in on youth for its driver line-up, it was obviously a terrible experience, but a cash-strapped holding pattern year with an undeveloped car driven by Mick Schumacher and Nikita Mazepin was a very different prospect to what Haas has got in store for 2027 with Bearman and Camara.

The fact that it held a proper old-school shootout for the seat with such a varied line-up of candidates makes it an even better story.

Camara has F1's most important trait

Camara getting a shot at F1 is richly deserved, and it's the kind of anti-conservatism driver choice that rival teams should take note of.

He's had a fascinating junior career so far, starting off in the (huge) shadow of Kimi Antonelli in Formula 4 and the Formula Regional European Championship.

But Camara didn't panic. He took the slow path, staying in FREC another year, growing as a driver and dominating that season before adding the Formula 3 crown one year later, while Antonelli made his F1 debut.

He arrived in F2 and demonstrated arguably the best raw pace in the category since Charles Leclerc.

There have been rough edges. He's not had the same devastating execution as the likes of Leclerc. But he shares the trait all successful F2-F1 graduates have had: sheer raw pace.

It's that speed that's prompted Haas to take a gamble on him, and it will be that speed that will go a long way to helping Camara establish himself in F1.

title: Ferrari F1 junior Camara to race for Haas
author: Josh Suttill
text:
Ferrari protege Rafael Camara will make his Formula 1 debut in 2027 after signing a multi-year deal to race for Haas.

The team was blown away by Camara's performance in his Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outing with the team at Portimao in August, where he set an impressive pace in Haas's 2025 F1 car.

That helped Camara beat the likes of McLaren reserve driver Leonardo Fornaroli, Toyota's Ryo Hirakawa, and ex-Alpine F1 driver Jack Doohan in the race to replace incumbent Esteban Ocon.

Ocon's two years at Haas have fallen short of expectations as he has generally been outpaced by Ferrari junior Ollie Bearman.

The Race revealed Haas would split with Ocon during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, where it was also known that Camara was the clear favourite to replace him.

Camara won back-to-back titles in the Formula Regional European Championship (an intermediate step between Formula 4 and Formula 3) and F3 in consecutive years before stepping up to Formula 2 in 2026.

The 21-year-old Brazilian currently leads a closely contested F2 championship with two scheduled rounds (Qatar and Abu Dhabi) remaining.

He has won three races and has had a standout qualifying average of 2.54, but it’s been far from a straightforward campaign, with Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu even referencing Camara's tricky weekends - he made a mistake that cost him victory in Monaco and made another costly error in Montreal - in Haas's announcement.

"I'm really excited to sign such a young, amazing talent like Rafael Camara," Komatsu said.

"I don't need to tell everyone about his achievements in the junior formulas, it's been very impressive, and in his rookie season in Formula 2, the speed he's shown in some very difficult moments, like qualifying in Monaco and Montreal - that all goes to show the potential Rafa has.

"He showed when we had him drive in our TPC programme in Portugal that he could handle himself very well [and] with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed.

"Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special."

Camara has been a member of the Ferrari driver academy since he was in karting in 2021, and will graduate to F1 as its most decorated junior driver ever.

Should Camara win a third consecutive (main season) junior single-seater title, he'll be the first since Oscar Piastri won FREC-F3-F2 in 2019-21.

Camara said he was "very happy" to be joining Haas and thanked Komatsu and Haas F1 team owner Gene Haas for the trust they had placed in him.

"I'm also very grateful to the Scuderia Ferrari driver academy for their support and for everything they have contributed to my development over the years, as well as to my family for always being there throughout this journey," Camara said.

"Now my focus is on preparing myself in the best possible way for this new challenge. There will be a lot to learn, and I'm looking forward to working closely with the team, understanding the car and continuing to develop as a driver."

There is no official confirmation, but Bearman is expected to be retained and form an all-Ferrari-junior line-up alongside Camara.

Komatsu has repeatedly affirmed that those Ferrari links have not influenced Haas's 2026 driver line-up and Camara has been chosen completely on merit.

title: Champions League review: PSG’s benchmark, Viking uprising and an Italian-German dilemma
author: John Brewin
text:
The competition returned after the international break as the reigning champions put on a devastating display and Italy looked for its next savior

Famous faces in the crowd for English teams’ home matches on Wednesday. While Prince William delighted in his beloved Aston Villa’s 6-0 romp over Fenerbahce , Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City homecoming was spoiled by Paris Saint-Germain showing they still represent the benchmark in European club football this season.

The center-circle inquest led by Erling Haaland after Vitinha put PSG 3-0 up was a jarring contrast to the triumphalism shown when City were winning at Liverpool last weekend. The Parisians put on a devastating display in the first half and, although the defiance City exhibited at Anfield on Sunday was on display again in the second half, PSG held on for a 4-2 win. “We could’ve lost this match if they scored the chances they created,” said a magnanimous Luis Enrique.

City may soon be absent from the competition, after they were found guilty of more than 100 charges of breaking the Premier League’s financial regulations. If City wish to sign off with a valedictory trophy lift they now know the standard they must meet – and beat. PSG have had their own issues with financial regulations in the era of petrodollar state ownership but, with the club president Nasser Al-Khelaifi a major powerbroker in European football, they have become an establishment club. While City are now pariahs, PSG have become near untouchables, not least on the field of play.

“He who brings glory to Rome, Rome honors for ever,” read a banner in the Stadio Olimpico. “Your hands are blessed and the people will give you eternal glory!” José Mourinho won hearts during his time in charge of Roma. But his popularity ratings are nowhere near as high in Madrid, though the manner of Real Madrid’s 4-3 comeback win over Roma will calm the gathering storm he has faced since returning to work for Florentino Pérez. The comeback came via Madrid’s next generation: Carlos Espí, 21, pulled the scoreline back to 3-2; the unlikely aerial threat of the 5ft 8in Endrick, 20, made it 3-3; and Antonio Rüdiger scored the winner, via a second assist for Arda Güler, 21. Mourinho embracing youth is a fresh development. This week saw Mourinho block a loan move to Milan for Endrick, and he admitted in Rome: “The first half was the coach’s fault; the second half was the players’ fault.”

A record 78 goals flew in this game week; the previous record was 71. On the wrong end were the Serie A clubs. In addition to Roma’s defeat, Como lost 3-2 at Feyenoord, the decisive moment coming via an own-goal for Robert Sánchez, the keeper loaned from Chelsea. Inter also lost, 4-3 to Club Brugge, whose performances in the competition in recent years meant the result was not much of a surprise. Napoli lost 3-1 to Villarreal, the Yellow Submarines’ first Champions League win in eight matches. Neapolitan focus was on a running battle between Massimiliano Allegri, the Napoli coach, and Kevin De Bruyne. Scott McTominay’s return to the team has pushed De Bruyne deeper. The Belgian made clear his feelings on playing there with some highly demonstrative body language.

There were two hat-tricks this week. Bradley Barcola ignited his Liverpool career with a treble at Lask, whose defending during their 6-3 defeat was suboptimal to say the least. That 4-3 Brugge win was mostly thanks to Nicolò Tresoldi. The striker was born in Italy, but moved to Hanover when he was 13, and he plays for Germany’s under-21s. Italian soul-searching after missing out on the last three World Cups has cast Tresoldi as a new savior. “I always speak Italian at home; I was born in Italy too,” he said post-match. “We’ll see.”

Paolo Di Canio, on Sky Italia, was pessimistic: “He has already chosen.”

After Bodø/Glimt’s exploits over the last couple of seasons and the national team’s admirable World Cup showing, the true football hipsters have a new destination in Norway. Viking play a thousand miles south-west of Bodø, in Norway’s oil capital, Stavanger. The club has co-managers in Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim and Morten Jensen: the pair were interviewed for the top job before deciding it was best they share duties. Viking are in the Champions League for the first time since the 1992-93 season, and at one point on Tuesday the Eliteserien champions led Bayern Munich 2-0. But a seismic shock was averted via two Harry Kane goals and another from Luis Díaz that put Bayern 3-2 up. Once Herman Haugen headed home at the back post, Viking had rescued a point with a 3-3 draw. “I could have played another 90 minutes,” said the captain, Zlatko Tripić, “I’m so incredibly proud.”

“I expect more. I’m not going to close my mouth; we need more ambition, we need to talk more about winning Champions Leagues and Premier Leagues in terms of other things.” Lisandro Martínez was undeterred by Peter Schmeichel’s soft-shoe questioning on Tuesday’s CBS broadcast after Manchester United’s defeat to Atlético Madrid.

“If we don’t say the truth, nothing will change,” added Martínez, whose Manchester United contract expires in June. Martínez’s interventions exposed the cracks at United – and highlighted the dubious merits of having a football celebrity do a journalist’s job.

A quick turnaround sees the third round staged next week, with Manchester United heading to Como for another examination of Michael Carrick’s regime. That follows a difficult Sunday trip to Leeds for United.…

title: What you need to know about F1's new driver - Rafael Camara
author: Josh Suttill
text:
- Rafael Camara is Formula 1's newest driver as he'll form part of Haas's 2027 driver line-up.

Back in Azerbaijan - where it emerged Camara was highly likely to replace Esteban Ocon - Josh Suttill spoke to Camara and his Invicta F2 team boss James Robinson to find out more about his 2026 season and how he feels being on the brink of F1.

You can read the article below, first published in September 2026.

"I've never met a driver who is so naturally talented as he is."

If you speak to anyone who has worked with likely 2027 Formula 1 driver Rafael Camara, you'll get a similar response to the above.

Humble and softly-spoken out of the car, Camara can be ruthlessly fast inside the cockpit, delivering qualifying laps that blow his rivals out of the water, but with the racecraft of a rough diamond.

The chief characteristic that has fundamentally made Camara an F2 title contender this year and explains why he's impressed Haas enough to consider signing him is that he's .

Just look at the qualifying average from F2 this season and rookie Camara's advantage is clear, with only second-year driver Alex Dunne coming close.

1 Rafael Camara 2.542 Alex Dunne 3.774 Martinius Stenshorne 7.546 Joshua Duerksen 8.388 Dino Beganovic 9.23 9 Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak 10.38

10 Gabriele Mini 10.92

You have to go back to 2021 F2 champion Oscar Piastri to find a driver pick up so many poles (five) in F2 as a rookie and for a driver with a better average qualifying record.

It was that searing raw speed that was also the bedrock of his 2025 Formula 3 title campaign, too, as he was on pole for four of the first five feature races.

"The speed is just incredible. I've never met a driver who is so naturally talented as he is. He has a feeling for the tyres I've never seen before. It's so natural," Camara's Invicta F2 team boss Robinson told The Race.

"As soon as he stepped in the car, you could see that this guy had something, had a natural speed and feel that we hadn't seen before."

That's strong praise from an Invicta team that has run Audi F1 driver Gabriel Bortoleto and McLaren reserve (and fellow 2027 Haas F1 seat contender) Leonardo Fornaroli to F2 titles in 2024 and 2025.

Invicta had plenty of drivers offering their services for 2026, but Camara's raw speed had been so impressive even before F3, he'd long been on the team's radar.

Camara is by no means the finished article. Much like the last Ferrari junior to graduate to F1, Ollie Bearman (ironically Camara's likely 2027 team-mate), alongside the insane raw speed there are still rough edges to his racecraft, by his own admission.

His speed in F2 has been present since pre-season testing, but his early season was blighted by major errors in Montreal and Monaco.

In Montreal, he spun himself out by diving down the inside of fellow Ferrari junior Dino Beganovic into Turn 2 when the door was already closed.

And then in Monaco, Camara lost a near-certain win by struggling to fire up his tyres on the outlap after his pitstop and then locking up and going down the escape road at Turn 1 while under pressure from title rival Nikola Tsolov.

"We can be quite happy with what we have done this year, but for sure there were some moments that could be easily avoided," Camara told The Race.

"Some mistakes that I think maybe cost us a bit too much points. There was Montreal that I think was a really stupid move.

"Then Monaco, in a way, we had everything so under control. This year the outlap was very tricky. By being a bit more on the safe side, I snowballed. Then after it was a big problem.

"We know that Monaco is impossible to overtake, so I didn't want to lose the race. Then I ended up in a much worse place than just being P2.

"But overall I think it has been a very good season, because I think every time that we had done a mistake, or something that was not the ideal thing or the right thing, we've always been able to learn and to grow.

"This is how I really see this season, I think I really grew as a driver, also with the team, getting more comfortable with everyone."

Camara hasn't been able to completely cut out the errors - despite following up that rough early patch with inspired wins at Barcelona and Spa.

The Madring feature race perfectly summed up the duality of his racecraft, as having pulled off a remarkably bold move on his title rival Tsolov, Camara followed it up by going a step too far with a bolder move that sent Oliver Goethe into the wall and earned Camara a 10-second time penalty.

"He's generally a very calm head in the car and doesn't often make mistakes," Robinson said.

"He has made a couple this year. I think the downfall, if you compare it to, say, Leonardo [Fornaroli, 2025 F2 champion] last season, the big difference between those two years, Leo didn't make any big mistakes at all. That was the recipe for him winning the championship with a round to spare.

"Rafa has a speed that is undeniable. He's worked hard this year. All he needed to do really was just cut out those silly mistakes that cost him in Montreal and Monaco, for example, and get off the line well.

"If he can do those things, then he's pretty good at winning races."

Baku was another example, as after his sprint race was ruined by picking up a 10-second time penalty for locking up and running into the back of Aston Martin junior Mari Boya, Camara rebounded brilliantly on Saturday to win the second feature race and jump back into the points lead.

Camara's conversations with his Invicta race engineer Pau Rivera, who has engineered the likes of Bortoleto and Zhou Guanyu on their way to F1, have been popular additions to F2's highlight reels this year.

In Montreal, Rivera told Camara: "That's not the way, mate, that's not the way, so now you need to keep it cool and reset" and after Camara lost the Monaco win, he remarkably asked Camara over the radio: "What was the issue on this lap? Why the f*** did you go so slow? We had a massive margin! What the f*** happened there?"

Those conversations drew plenty of attention on social media, but for Camara it's simply evidence of an honest relationship between driver and race engineer.

"Since the beginning we always had a very nice relationship, we've always been very transparent to each other," Camara explained.

"In the races and the sessions, we're both more excited, and I think sometimes if we don't do the perfect job or if we don't maximise, for sure we're going to be a bit upset.

"Probably in those moments we can discuss a bit more. But it's still nothing really personal. It's just us trying to always maximise and do the best of what we can do together."

Asked if Camara was ready for F1, Robinson replied: "100%. I'd be very, very surprised if he doesn't race in Formula 1".

Camara is yet to partake in an F1 practice session, but he has been clocking plenty of laps for both Ferrari and Haas as part of their Testing of Previous Cars programmes - teams are allowed to test pre-2026 cars on up to 20 days this year, with race drivers limited to 1000km total mileage.

It was Camara's speed he showed Haas, which also tried out Jack Doohan, Fornaroli and reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa, in the TPC tests that has been a huge factor in him becoming the favourite to replace Ocon.

Camara said of his TPC running: "The tests we did with the TPCs have been always positive.

"I was able always to learn and to grow up during these tests…I'm pleased with what I did.

"Also, it was very nice to get this amount of tests [in] F1, so also in a way for us to be more prepared and in a good shape."

So would Camara be ready for F1 if he was given a race seat for 2027?

He replies: "Yes, I don't see why not. I think at the end of the day you're [still] driving fast cars in a circuit [in F1]. So I've been doing this for quite a while.

"It's a very different place. There's a lot more things going on. But I think that it's more really outside of the car.

"In the car, you just do your job and try to always maximise what you can. I think it's the thing that I enjoy the most. It will be always a pleasure to be driving.

"If I'm there it's also a dream, because you're working your whole life for that.

"Obviously it's always nice to get TPCs, but you don't want to just get the taste and not be there the whole time.

"It will be something nice and I think I'm ready."

title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
text:
The UK's economy recorded surprise growth in August despite the impact of rising energy prices and borrowing costs.

Official figures showed the economy expanded by 0.1% in the month, defying analysts' expectations of a slight contraction.

It means the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August, and follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Chancellor John Healey, who will deliver his first Budget in two weeks, said the UK has shown resilience in the face of conflicts in Europe and the Middle East.

Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply.

The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted.

Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period.

But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period.

August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%.

Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought".

He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs".

PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance.

"The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added.

The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations.

Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks.

"This week the IMF have upgraded UK growth for 2026 and said that our fiscal discipline stands out with the lowest deficit in the G7 forecast by 2029."

He promised to build on the UK's debt reduction plans, which were praised by the IMF, and use the Budget to "provide some breathing space for today, and offer fresh hope for the future".

The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing."

He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape.

title: 'Fourth place almost feels like a small victory' - Fabio Jakobsen starts to bounce back in Guangxi
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Once one of the world’s preeminent sprinters, winning bunch kicks in a variety of races and topping the points classification in the 2021 Vuelta a España, the 30-year-old former Dutch champion has a total of 46 wins to his name.

However, in recent years the Visma-Lease a Bike rider has regressed into a shadow of his former self, with his most recent victory as far back as April 2024. Thursday’s result was his best WorldTour placing since the UAE Tour in February of that year.

Suffering illnesses and injury, including iliac artery endofibrosis, Jakobsen was often unable to finish races, let alone contest the sprint, and while his results were tailing off towards the end of his time with Soudal-QuickStep, his loss of form coincided with a move to what is now Picnic-Post NL.

In more than four years with the team, he managed only one victory. However, a mid-season move to Visma over the summer seems to have sparked something in Jakobsen.

Since joining the team on August 14th, he has won two national-level races and has begun clawing his way up results boards, drawing praise from his sports director in Guangxi, Gaëton Pons.

"This fourth place almost feels like a small victory when you consider where Fabio has come from," Pons said. "In his last four races with the team, he has achieved his four best results of the season. Physically, he's not back to his previous level yet, but we're clearly seeing progress. He wants to fight again, enjoys racing, and is showing a lot of confidence. That's an important step toward next season."

Seeing Jakobsen slipping out the back of the bunch whenever the road tilted uphill had become a sad but familiar sight, so the team hadn’t identified Thursday’s 212.3km stage, which included almost 1,800m of climbing, as one for him, but he defied expectations, playing a full part in the final.

"He managed to survive the climbs thanks to the support of his teammates. In the finale, the guys did an excellent job. Fabio himself mentioned that it had been a long time since he'd had such a good lead-out. Owain [Doull], in particular, did a fantastic job in the final meters."

Friday’s stage is hillier, and Jakobsen is highly unlikely to be able to fight for the win, though Saturday’s fifth stage could present another chance.

title: Eneco Tour: Jakob Söderqvist doubles up with dominant stage 2 time trial victory, extends race lead
author: James Moultrie
text:
Jakob Söderqvist (Lidl-Trek) doubled up on victories at the Eneco Tour , adding the stage 2 individual time trial to his prologue success in the Netherlands on Thursday.

In a close-fought battle over the flat 13.6km course in Tilburg, Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) had set the best time and held off a powerful charge from Ethan Hayter (Soudal-QuickStep) by less than half a second, but the Swedish rider was simply too fast and knocked him off the hot seat as the last starter.

Almost crashing as getting on the power too early caused him to pedal strike around one of the final corners, Söderqvist stayed up and arrived at the line in a time of 15:04 to beat Fisher-Black by 11 seconds, also the only rider to average more than 54kph throughout his effort.

With a small hop over the line, the Swede netted the eighth win of his career and sixth in a time trial as a professional, also extending his overall lead of the race to 14 seconds from Hayter and 15 from Fisher-Black.

"It was a fast one, actually; I think I experienced it faster than I expected beforehand. I didn't feel too much headwind even though we were talking about it a lot before, so it was just a good day, and I cannot say much more than that," said Söderqvist.

"It was nice corners, kept you on your toes a bit – how I like it – and it was a bigger pleasure than normally."

He'll look to defend his orange jersey in the remaining three stages, with punchy routes and some likely breathless racing standing in his way of the overall title on Sunday. Sat in eighth overall, 29 seconds down, Christophe Laporte (Visma-Lease a Bike) looks the most likely rider to challenge Söderqvist for the overall.

"For sure I'm happy. Everything so far is as good as we could ever expect. I was strong in this race also last year, so we know it suits me really well, but I'm happy the shape is still here with me this time of year, and we hope to keep it," he said.

"The pressure will be on, and we know how good people like Christophe Laporte are on Vam Berg," who won his European title there in 2023, "and even tomorrow will already be a lot of pressure from the other teams who believe. We are here to fight, and this is how we need to pursue."

Racing continued at the Eneco Tour with Milan De Ceuster (Picnic PostNL) leading the 87 riders off the start ramp of the stage 2 individual time trial in reverse GC order.

An early benchmark was set by Steffen De Schuyteneer (Lotto Intermarché) with a time of 15:46 over the 13.6-kilometre course in Tilburg, until he was beaten by Milan Lanhove (Team Flanders-Baloise), who went eight seconds quicker.

As a result of the opening day's prologue, most of the top time trial riders were placed inside the top 10 on GC, so Lanhove would have known his time was vulnerable, and it was Victor Campenaerts (Visma-Lease a Bike) who knocked him off the hot seat by 11 seconds – but there were several riders going even faster on the course.

Among those ahead of Campenaerts at the intermediate check were his Visma teammate Edoardo Affini and Kristian Egholm (Lidl-Trek Future Racing), but both lost out by more than 10 seconds after a rapid final run to the line by the Belgian.

Pepijn Reinderink (Soudal Quick-Step) was the first rider to average more than 53kph over the course, knocking Campenaerts out of the top spot, with just eight riders still to come in. But it wasn't long before Fisher-Black scorched to the line four seconds quicker than the Dutchman.

Hayter ran him close, missing out on the lead by less than half a second, but the prologue winner and pre-stage favourite Söderqvist was powering through the course, clocking through the intermediate check five seconds faster than the Kiwi.

Söderqvist ramped up his speed and the risk, almost coming unstuck before the final kilometre, but he kept it together to convincingly beat everyone by more than 10 seconds.

'It became a dictatorship' – Extensive report on alleged culture of fear leads Picnic-PostNL to launch independent investigation
author: James Moultrie
text:
WorldTour team Picnic PostNL will commission an "independent, professional investigation into our team culture" after an extensive report in Dutch media revealed alleged toxic working conditions in recent years, which one former coach described as a "dictatorship".

revealed the findings of their investigative report on Thursday morning, conducted over several months in 2026, into the culture that developed under sports director Rudi Kemna and team owner Iwan Spekenbrink.

The two media outlets spoke with 71 current or former employees of the team, most of them being quoted anonymously, to paint a picture of an alleged "culture of fear" and an "unsafe working situation".

Picnic-PostNL issued a statement on Thursday, saying "we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications", but nevertheless acknowledging that "it is important to take a critical look at ourselves" in light of the reported findings.

"The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for," read the statement.

"We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL."

What exactly has been said about the culture in the team?

The most striking claim of a toxic culture came from retired professional rider Martijn Tusveld, who raced in the team's colours for seven seasons, first as Sunweb and then as DSM between 2018 and 2024. He highlighted how his standing in the team changed when – after being asked for his opinion by Kemna – he openly criticised the team's tactics at the Giro d'Italia in 2020.

Tusveld was reportedly told he was creating a "negative atmosphere" and would later tell Kemna directly, in a 2025 email, that after the Giro incident he no longer dared to speak up, feeling "powerless", and even that he was not the person he once was.

"I became anxious," he told . "I thought: I'll keep my mouth shut and say yes and amen. And that's what I did for the rest of the years with this team."

Tusveld also said he suffered with symptoms of depression in 2021, stating: "I also thought about harming myself."

Just one account of the 71, similar experiences to Tusveld's about a shift in the team's culture were detailed by anonymous former staff members in the report.

Tom Dumoulin's former coach Adriaan Helmantel was another who spoke on the record, claiming that Dumoulin's landmark victory at the Giro d'Italia in 2017 did mark a turning point for the team, but not in the way it should have.

As Helmantel saw it, the management looked to exert excessive influence, wanting everything to trickle down from the top, as "they started becoming paranoid" of riders "calling the shots" if riders and coaches became too close.

"It became a dictatorship," Helmantel said.

In a separate report from , former rider Nicolas Roche, who also rode for Team Sky and Saxo Bank, issued a striking statement: "I think this management is not suitable for cycling," said the Irishman.

"In cycling, we have to deal with a lot of variables. It is not a predictable sport. The body is not a perfect machine. We have to deal with the weather conditions and also the tactics of 24 other teams. I understand that people want a master plan to be prepared, but they cannot plan the 17th stage of the Tour de France as early as May. And that is what they did."

Roche claimed that he was "pushed towards the exit" in 2021 and that he was told he had "too much influence on the young riders", stating: "My experience became a problem for the management."

In their statement, Picnic-PostNL said: "If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened."

Team dispute claims they didn't engage with investigation

While Picnic-PostNL have now issued a statement and vowed to launch an internal investigation in direct response to the report from and they have disputed the two publications' claims that they refused to engage with the investigation.

claim that they approached the team for comment in response to their findings on October 12, and then approached the team management in-person two days later, stating: " and gave owner Iwan Spekenbrink the opportunity at the Picnic-PostNL headquarters in Deventer to respond regarding the WorldTour team's working methods. Spekenbrink proved unwilling to do so and ultimately chose not to respond at all. Neither in writing nor on camera."

Picnic PostNL have a differing view on how attempts at conversation played out once presented with the investigation, as referenced in their statement.

"According to , it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this.

"Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with . These attempts were unsuccessful."

Picnic-PostNL's statement in full

We have taken note of the publications by NOS Sport and In de Waaier about Team Picnic PostNL. The accounts shared by current and former riders and staff members affect us. At the same time, we do not recognise ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications.

The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.

The team and our three promises

Since the team was founded in 2008, three promises have formed the foundation of our approach to professional cycling.

The first promise: fair, healthy and responsible sport.

Our anti-doping policy is an important part of this promise. It is not only about what we communicate externally, but also about the mindset and ethical considerations that guide our decisions in practice.

The second promise: safe collaboration based on shared values.

We want everyone within the team, on and off the bike, to be treated with respect and to feel free to express an opinion, encourage one another, ask questions and raise concerns. Mutual commitment and integrity are central to this, helping us create an environment where people can develop, perform and enjoy working together.

The third promise: continuity and job security.

We have made a commitment to do everything we can to secure the future of the team and, in doing so, preserve jobs within professional cycling.

While this may sound self-evident, job security in professional cycling is anything but. The sport’s economic model falls seriously short. Every year, several teams disappear, with the associated loss of jobs. This has become almost normal, even though it should never be the case in a sport of this scale.

That is why we have been working to secure the future of the team since 2008. Over the years, we have provided employment for hundreds of people.

According to NOS, it spent months trying to speak with current and former riders and staff members. As soon as we received indications that the investigation was taking place, we offered to meet with NOS to discuss our philosophy and vision, and to give the broadcaster the opportunity to speak with current team members and colleagues. NOS chose not to take up that offer. We regret this.

Last Monday, we were then given only a few days to respond to a number of questions, either in writing or on camera. In response, we made several further attempts to speak with NOS. These attempts were unsuccessful.

Independent investigation into team culture

In a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organisation or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.

We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.

We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may be needed, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.

title: Should you rethink the cycling kit you're buying? Why circularity could be the future of sustainable clothing
author: Emma Cole
text:
According to the European Environment Agency (EEA), each European citizen throws away an average of 16kg of textiles each year. The EEA estimates almost 75% of this is incinerated or ends up in landfill, and some is shipped to Asia and Africa.

The reality of this is shocking. I’ve seen it first-hand at markets in Tunisia where hundreds of tables of clothing are piled high and sold for a few pounds, and global fast fashion brands do the same thing but on a much, much bigger scale around the world.

Albeit smaller than the big fast fashion manufacturers, cycling clothing is also part of this conversation, especially given the constant flow of new collection launches, designs and colourways.

The UN Environment Programme says 2-8% of CO2 emissions come from the textile industry, while the Ellen MacArthur Foundation says that only 1% of clothing is circular.

Circularity refers to the concept of keeping clothing in use for as long as possible, through reuse, repair, and recycling, essentially a loop, and eliminating waste. By comparison, the traditional manufacturing model is linear: clothing is sold to be worn and then disposed of, often without regard for repair and reuse.

Circularity has yet to become mainstream in the clothing industry, let alone the cycling kit sector, but French brand Velor is trying to change that. We spoke to Velor and other voices in the cycling industry to learn more about the future of sustainable clothing, and how cyclists can join that movement.

A world-first 'circular' cycling jersey

Velor, a brand founded in France in 2021, has created the first circular cycling jersey made from textile waste, could represent a major step forward for both the sportswear and textile industries. It took five years from concept to bringing the jersey to market, because Velor had to build every step from scratch.

"We started from nothing, and we had to build it ourselves," says Florian Jardin, who co-founded Velor with his brother Mickael.

"The whole value chain is very complicated because you start with low volumes, you grow step by step, and it's not standard fabrics."

The brand’s supply chain starts in France and the Netherlands with clothing collection, and heads through France, Germany, Spain, and Portugal for the final product, before closing the loop by returning to the collection stage.

Velor scaled its circular jersey gradually, from lab-testing a single jersey, to recycling 300 jerseys two years ago, to now processing at the one-tonne scale.

The brand also worked with Maastricht University and its suppliers to understand the impact of its jersey and to quantify the life cycle assessment data. Jardin says the result is an infinitely recyclable jersey, made from 85% textile waste and a footprint of 0.9kg CO2 equivalent.

"If you look at a jersey made in China, the emissions are 3-4kg for an equivalent jersey with the same fabric, weight and construction," he adds.

Another non-traditional business model is using a pre-order system, which requires customers to wait for their kit to be made, but allows brands to produce only as much as they need.

Bristol-based brand Kostüme produces kits solely via pre-order. Founder Ed Bartlett says a pre-order model removes the waste which is baked into the traditional retail model.

"A lot of brands are trying to solve the wrong part of the problem by focusing on recycled fabrics and repair capabilities, but the problem is we're making too much stuff," says Bartlett.

"The research that I've done suggests 30% of products get sold at full price, 30% get sold at a discount, 40% don't ever get sold, and then a lot of brands have a 40% return rate, so even the stuff that they're selling gets returned, and these are big numbers.

"If you can cut that by even 10% or 20%, that has a much bigger impact than anything else."

Bartlett says his 55% returning customer rate and 100% year-on-year growth are proof that the pre-order model works.

Kostüme also doesn’t carry the cost of unsold stock which gives Bartlett flexibility. For example, Kostüme’s bib shorts use a separately applied gripper that adds two weeks to production time and costs more but virtually eliminates fabric waste.

The few items that aren't sold or are returned go to their Ready to Ship store, offering customers a chance to buy an item with a faster turn around time.

Swiss brand Assos recently tested the pre-order model through a jersey collaboration with One Garment at a Time (OGAT).

"The OGAT project was a way to test a new business model that brings us closer to the customer, letting us plan and produce with the goal of zero waste and zero excess stock," says Davide Colletto, quality, safety and environment manager at Assos.

"It is a more sustainable approach, and we are evaluating how this model could be extended to other parts of our range where it makes sense."

Why aren’t more brands trying to close the loop and reduce waste?

In the early days of Velor, Jardin reached out to many of the major brands in the hope of partnering with them, but he didn’t get much engagement.

"I spoke to all of them, but they said they weren’t interested, didn’t have time or it wasn’t in their strategy," he says.

He says cost was also a reason. Producing circular fabric costs about 11 times more than sourcing fabric from China, while manufacturing in Portugal costs five to six times more than in China, according to Jardin.

Jardin built these costs into the business from the start, but for bigger brands there would be a large cost for them to pivot their business model.

"The circular economy needs to deliver cheap products, and that means scaling up and getting the economies of scale", says Dr Sam Hampton, a lecturer and researcher in Environmental Governance and Behaviour Energy programme at the University of Oxford.

But, as Velor shows, that doesn’t exist yet.

Dr Hampton suggests a carbon tax on virgin raw materials which could be a lever to make recycled alternatives comparatively cheaper.

"You need to change the whole system in multiple ways, make the virgin competitors more expensive and the recycled competitive products cheaper, but that's a system-wide global challenge."

The domination of the traditional model means pivoting is difficult.

"The linear model still dominates the industry, but it's becoming harder to justify environmentally, commercially and in regulation," says Sam Wrest, senior ESG manager at Rapha.

"Circularity is the direction we're moving in, but in cycling apparel it comes with real technical challenges."

The technical challenges revolve around the difficulties of recycling mixed materials.

"Cycling kit relies on elastane blends, bonded seams, silicone grippers and chamois pads, which are very hard to recycle back into new fibre," explains Wrest. "Textile-to-textile recycling for these materials isn't commercially viable at scale yet."

Wrest says Rapha is exploring this area nonetheless, and expects to share more soon, but its current focus remains on durability, repairs and its trade-in service to extend the lives of existing garments. Danish brand Pas Normal Studios echoes these challenges.

"Right now, the most effective lever within our control is keeping products in use for longer, through quality, repairs and spare parts," says Fabian Pirrwitz, Impact and responsibility analyst at Pas Normal Studios.

Moving to mono-material – garments made exclusively of one fabric – is also not a straightforward solution, particularly not when it comes to technical or high-performance cycling clothing.

"Mono-material fabrics can make recycling easier, but the recycling and recovery infrastructure is still limited and not yet fully developed," adds Colletto of Assos.

"Different garments have different technical requirements, and a single material is not always the best way to achieve the performance, comfort and durability we need."

The challenges don't stop there, either. There is also the issue of synthetic fibres shedding microplastics during washing, and the long-term impact of things like PFAs, which were previously used extensively in cycling clothing and waterproofs. Whilst many brands are trying, the task of making cycling clothing sustainable and environmentally friendly is far from simple.

While Velor and Kostüme openly talk about their supply chains, some brands shy away from transparency over where your clothes come from and how they are made.

Several mainstream cycling brands operate with supply chains in China and Vietnam. Maap, Decathlon (Van Rysel) and Rapha manufacture some products in Asia.

Decathlon brand Van Rysel has removed carbon emissions information from its website for many of its jerseys, and some of its latest products don’t have any environmental initiatives linked to them, giving the impression that the brand is scaling back on its transparency and sustainability.

One Decathlon jersey still listed with emissions comes in at 4.9kg CO2 equivalent. We approached Van Rysel for comment, but did not receive a response in time for publication.

An upcoming EU regulation called the Digital Product Passport (DPP) scheme could change this lack of transparency in the world of cycling clothing. The DPP will require all textiles sold in the EU to include data across supply chains such as material, chemicals, origin, and recyclability. It is expected to apply by the end of 2029.

"I think what we need is more transparency… A name and a company for every step of the process," says Jardin.

Fabric certifications such as Bluesign and OEKO-TEX are often used to imply sustainability credentials, but they're not the be-all and end-all, and certainly don't cover all factors of production.

"A certified fabric doesn't tell you a brand's overall carbon footprint, the full picture of how workers are treated, or what happens to products when they reach the end of their life," says Wrest.

"Certifications are useful for managing specific risks in the supply chain, but they're a starting point, not proof of sustainability."

A more circular and less wasteful future?

With the recent record-breaking heatwaves and ongoing climate crisis, it would be logical for consumer habits to change – not just as shoppers all wake up to the impact that unsustainable consumption and business practices can have on the world around, but in response to climate change itself.

Dr Hampton predicts a drive for new lighter summer kit which performs in the heat, rather than less buying overall, for example.

For traditional business models, upcoming regulation will force them to pivot to more transparent practices, but the costs of going circular and lack of recycling infrastructure remain significant hurdles for many brands.

However, Velor’s innovation with an infinitely recyclable jersey shows us what is possible and showcases how a circular clothing economy could work.

Similarly, Kostüme’s business success highlights a consumer desire for a different way of thinking, but both Kostüme and Velor are small parts of a much wider and impactful cycling clothing ecosystem.

"We’re a drop in the ocean ultimately, but hopefully we can scale this to a point where it’s inarguable, and people can’t shy away from it," says Bartlett.

But with major player Assos testing the waters with pre-order, and Rapha focusing on garment longevity, perhaps the future of cycling clothing is a little bit rounder after all.

title: AI giant Anthropic woos potential investors ahead of stock market debut
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw its revenue surge by 45% to $16.8bn (£12.7bn) in the three months to the end of September, the BBC understands.

The figures were reportedly revealed by the Claude-developer as it briefed prospective investors on Wednesday at its headquarters in San Francisco as it lays the groundwork for a stock market listing, which is expected to take place before the end of the year.

It comes as some tech stocks, including firms that make the chips and other hardware that power data centres, have come under pressure over concerns about the large amounts of money being spent on AI infrastructure.

An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.

Anthropic's revenue has risen in successive quarters this year, from $4.7bn in the first three months to $11.6bn the following period.

The company also reportedly said that it made a profit for the second quarter in a row.

Its revenue figures, along with those of rival OpenAI, offer an important gauge of the AI industry's growth and ability to finance the infrastructure needed to develop the technology.

Stocks in some US technology companies fell on Wednesday over concerns around investments in AI.

Share in chip makers - including AMD, Nvidia and Intel - fell sharply.

In Asia, shares in Japanese tech investment firm Softbank fell by 9% on Thursday morning. South Korean semiconductor giants were also down, with Samsung falling by 8.4% and SK Hynix dropping by more than 6%.

South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi index was 7.6% lower in morning trading.

The falls come after remarks by Hock Tan, the chief executive of US tech manufacturer Broadcom, over AI spending.

How backlash against data centres could shape the US midterm elections

'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire

Tan said at an conference in Singapore on Monday that many investors have "no clue" and have set "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino".

There also been concerns over the safety of AI models.

OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said in September that his company will not go public this year as it addresses concerns about the technology's safety.

The ChatGPT-developer is also eyeing a bumper stock market listing, which is expected to value the firm at more than $1tn.

Anthropic has also been vocal about AI's risks, with its chief executive Dario Amodei calling on the pace of development to slow down .

The company has continued expanding globally, opening an office in Singapore on Wednesday.

title: Man Utd a circus after Martinez comments - Keane
text:
Former captain Roy Keane says Manchester United are "like a circus" after defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's hierarchy.

Speaking after Tuesday's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad in the summer and "more from our technical director".

In a social media post on Wednesday he said he had spoken out of "anger and frustration".

The loss in Madrid stretched United's winless run to five games, and they have won just one of their opening six matches of the Premier League season.

Keane, speaking on The Overlap , external podcast, said Martinez's statement reflected the overall state of the club.

"There will be some fans saying it's great and some saying you're letting the team down, especially from a player who hasn't been at his best, when the team is struggling," he said.

"I think as a reflection of the club, it's obviously chaos there, like a bit of a circus.

"When you're going through a difficult spell like United are, the issue I have with certain players saying things is you always have to start with the man in the mirror before you start coming out with all these comments."

Outburst came out of 'anger and frustration' - Martinez

Wilcox the target again in another damaging Man Utd fallout

Man Utd defender Martinez issues scathing attack on board

Martinez, 28, is out of contract at the end of the season, though United have the option to extend his deal by another year.

"I don't think it will be a big falling-out - because I think we have question marks over this dressing room anyway," Keane said.

"I don't think there's enough characters - enough men in there - but I don't see him as a senior player at Manchester United . I see him as a centre-half who's making lots of mistakes."

Former United defender Gary Neville compared the incident to comments made by Wayne Rooney when they were team-mates in 2010.

Rooney pulled out of contract talks, saying he had not received "any of the assurances I was seeking about the future squad". Two days later he signed a five-year deal and later said staying was the best decision of his career.

"I've got a problem with this from a player's perspective," said Neville. "That is a direct attack on the players you are playing with.

"So if I were Harry Maguire or Bruno Fernandes, or any other senior player, I would be absolutely fuming with him because you're basically saying we shouldn't be here and we should be bringing more players in."

United travel to Leeds United in the Premier League on Sunday.

text:
Lieke Nooijen blasted to a second time trial stage win of the Eneco Tour Women on Thursday, overcoming some fierce competition in the stage 2 test in the Dutch town of Tilburg.

The Visma-Lease a Bike rider was the only competitor to stop the clock under 16 minutes over the 13.1km course, with Nienke Vinke (SD Worx-Protime) second, more than 20 seconds down, while stage 1 winner Sandrine Tas (Lotto-Intermarché) was third, a further second back.

Nooijen won the opening day’s prologue TT on Tuesday and now leads the GC standings, 20 seconds ahead of Tas, with Vinke third, with three stages left to race.

Nooijen has established herself as one of the best time trialists in the peloton this year and in this company was the clear favourite to win on Thursday. However, she will need to defend her lead on the ensuing stages, all of which have short punchy climbs, though the advantage she has built may well prove enough for her to take the overall come Sunday.

Nooijen had Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) not far in front as her carrot to chase, admitting that "Yes, of course, it always gives more motivation to beat her, and she was in front of me and came closer, but I didn’t catch her.

"It was hard, but I’m super happy to take my second victory on the TT bike here, and I had a lot of confidence since the time of the prologue," said Nooijen, with her eye on carrying the orange jersey all the way to the end.

"[There are] still three days to go. Also hard stages, so I think we can make a nice plan with our strong team, and also tomorrow it will be hard in Limburg, and then on Saturday on the Vam Berg, but you need to be sharp the whole race."

For its third day of racing, the Eneco Tour Women took on a 13.1km ITT effort with only 27m of elevation gain, almost completely flat, with a decent wind of around 15kph that was rarely at the riders’ back, though only with the first three kilometres into a full headwind.

First off the ramp was Austrian TT champion Christina Schweinberger, the Fenix-Premier Tech rider setting a time of 7:54 at the intermediate coming point and a finish time of 17:41. Second rider off was British new pro Robyn Clay (Picnic-PostNL), who stopped the clock just seven seconds slower than the Austrian, the two riders staying in first and second place respectively for some time.

Eventually Tess Moerman (AG Insurance-Soudal) overtook Clay before Slovakian champion Viktória Chladoňová (Visma-Lease a Bike) managed to usurp Schweinberger, having started as the 55th of the day’s 88 starters.

However, Chaladoňová was just the first of a number of faster times, with Silke Smulders (Liv-AlUla-Jayco), Femke De Vries (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Vinke all spending a while in the race lead until Nooijen overtook them all for victory.

title: ‘A Dictatorship’: Team Picnic-PostNL Rocked by Allegations of Culture of Fear
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Team Picnic-PostNL has promised to launch an independent investigation into shocking revelations unearthed by broadcaster NOS and the podcast In De Waaier.

The joint investigation by the two Dutch outlets exposed an atmosphere of fear, excessive control, and distrust that dates back more than a decade.

The project involved confidential interviews with 71 current and former Picnic-PostNL cycling team employees, and went live this week.

According to NOS , “many have terminated their employment traumatized. They speak of a ‘culture of fear’ and an ‘unsafe work situation.'”

The partnering men’s and women’s teams have seen superstar riders like Tom Dumoulin, Lorena Wiebes, and Romain Bardet on their books.

The embattled Picnic-PostNL team – which is currently dead last in both the men’s and women’s WorldTour rankings – rushed out a response Thursday.

The team said its offers to cooperate with the investigation by NOS and In De Waaier were ignored, and it promised “to commission an independent, professional investigation” into the allegations.

“In a performance-driven environment such as professional sport, things can go wrong. That is why there are several ways for people within our team to raise problems and concerns. Riders have a personal coach, there is a Rider Committee, and staff members can turn to confidential advisers. If people have felt unsafe within our organization or have felt they lacked sufficient opportunity to raise concerns, we want to understand how that could have happened.

“We are proud of what we have built since 2008 together with the many people who are, or have been, part of and associated with this team. Precisely for that reason, we believe it is important to take a critical look at ourselves.

“We will therefore commission an independent, professional investigation into our team culture. We will take its findings seriously and implement any improvements that may improvements, out of respect for everyone who is, or has been, part of Team Picnic PostNL.”

Picnic-PostNL, formerly known as Team Giant, Sunweb, and DSM, has been stalked by rumors of a controlling, authoritarian culture for years.

Riders have broken contracts amid reports of burnout. Tales have emerged of riders being punished for adjusting their saddle height without authorization, and being forbidden from eating a kiwi.

One anonymous athlete once branded life at the team as a “Soviet regime.”

The long-read investigation published by NOS on Thursday is the most damning indictment of the team yet.

It detailed management taking constructive feedback as an attack on the team’s philosophy. Interviewees described a demeaning attitude toward riders and an unwillingness to flex plans to meet personal needs.

“It became a dictatorship,” said former coach Adriaan Helmantel, who worked with Giro d’Italia winner Dumoulin, amongst others.

In its statement Thursday, Picnic-PostNL outlined its values of safety, collaboration, and fairness, and rejected the claims made in NOS and In De Waaier .

“We do not recognize ourselves in the overall picture presented in the publications,” reads the note.

“The fact that experiences differ does not diminish the seriousness of the accounts that have now come to light. We will therefore commission an independent investigation into how our team culture is experienced in practice and to what extent it reflects the culture we strive for.”

title: Conflicting reports surrounding the inclusion of the Montmartre climb on the final stage of the 2027 Tour de France route
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Editor's note: This article has been updated to reflect subsequent reports published in the French press.

Question marks have emerged concerning the future of the punchy Montmartre circuit that has shaken up the final stage of the Tour de France in the past two years, with conflicting reports in the French press surrounding its inclusion on the 2027 Tour de France route.

The route for the 2027 Tour de France will be unveiled in Paris next Thursday, and the newspaper reported this Thursday morning that the Montmartre climb is set to be excluded, meaning a return to a traditional flat-track sprint finish on the Champs Elysées.

However, this was later contradicted by separate reports from and , with both outlets reporting that the Classics-flavoured finale will be back for a third year of high drama and entertainment.

In the past two years, the Côte de la Butte Montmartre has shaken up the traditional format of the Tour's finale, measuring 1.1 km at an average gradient of 5.9%, mostly on cobblestones, and followed by a tricky little descent.

The organisers had already tweaked the format, extending the distance from the top of the climb to the finish line from six kilometres to just over 10km, which resulted in the closer contest between the attackers and the sprinters.

This appeared to strike a better balance between tradition and the modern desire for action and entertainment.

However, both editions were somewhat awkward, given that general classification timings have been neutralised on both occasions, with the GC 'frozen' and therefore finalised upon entry to the final circuit.

The final stage of the Tour has for many years been processional, with riders drinking champagne and posing for photographs in the early kilometres before racing in central Paris, but any situation where proper GC racing could see positions – or even the yellow jersey – change hands, would throw that celebratory atmosphere up in the air.

The last bunch sprint on the Champs Elysées came in 2023, with the 2024 edition moved from Paris entirely due to the Olympics taking place in the French capital that summer, and the Tour ending with a time trial in Nice.

It remains to be seen what the organisers do with stage 21 in the long-run, but more will become clear when we see what is officially confirmed for the final day of the 2027 Tour next Thursday.
